title: A pricing page for an independent school
metaTitle: What an independent school pricing page shows
excerpt: Show the annual fee, what it includes, what sits outside it, and how to visit or inquire. Parents use the page to judge fit, not to do long arithmetic.
alt: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it, laying out a fee in rows a family can scan.
caption: The sketch is a structure, not a speech. Fees should be a structure too. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a school fee page state?
faqs.answer: The annual fee by age or division, whether lunch, books, and ordinary trips are included, and the extras families actually meet: uniform, music lessons, exam entries, a bus. Date the page with the academic year. Two divisions with two fees need two lines.

faqs.question: Should aid be mentioned?
faqs.answer: If you offer a bursary, a sibling reduction, or nothing, say which. Explain who the conversation is for and how to start it. Do not publish a family's private award. Silence reads as maybe, and maybe fills the inbox with questions you cannot answer well.

faqs.question: How should the page hand off?
faqs.answer: Each fee block should lead to a visit, or to an inquiry when a visit is not possible yet. Carry the age so a junior fee does not dump a parent into a senior open morning. Link a PDF only after the on-page table is already enough, and only if the PDF matches.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An independent school pricing page is where a parent deciding where a child will spend years judges whether the fee fits the day, before they build a spreadsheet. Show what is included, what is not, and how to visit or inquire. If they will ask the shape of the price anyway, put that shape on the page.

People do not read a fee schedule as literature. Nielsen Norman Group found that visitors read only about a quarter of the text on pages they actually open. A pricing page that hides the annual figure inside a paragraph about values will be judged on whatever number happens to be visible, or it will lose to a school that states the figure and the extras in a list.

## Fit before the total

The parent is not ready to model eight years of inflation. They are asking a rougher question: is this the kind of school I thought it was, at a cost I can consider without a surprise in term two? A clear annual fee with lunch included is one product. The same day with lunch, trips, exam entries, and the uniform treated as surprises is a different product. The page exists to make that difference visible before anyone falls in love with a classroom.

Lead with the division or age range the homepage already showed, then the fee that belongs to it. If the junior school and the senior school are different numbers, they are different lines. A single "fees from" with no age attached teaches the wrong year, and the correction feels like a bait.

Judging fit is allowed to be quick. A short table beats a letter from the bursar. Age, what the year includes, what sits outside the fee, how to visit. A parent can compare that table with the other two schools. They cannot compare three essays about investment in the future.

Google's people-first guidance asks whether someone can leave having learned enough to reach their goal. On this page the goal is a yes, a no, or a "we should visit and then talk about aid." A page that withholds the shape of the fee fails that test, even when the prose is warm and the crest is sharp.

## What the fee has to include, by name

"Inclusive" is a claim. Make it a list the office already uses on the phone. Tuition for the stated year. Lunch, or not. Books, or not. The ordinary day trip, or not. After-school care until a named hour, or not. The items you are tired of explaining are the items that belong in the list. Fatigue is information.

Write each inclusion as a thing the family receives. "Hot lunch in the hall, every full day" is an inclusion. "A rich program" is not. The parent is trying to see whether the fee replaces a set of separate bills or only buys the lessons.

If something is included only for certain ages, say the ages in the same row. A reception year that includes care until 3, and a year-five fee that does not, will cause a bitter surprise if you blend them. Parents are planning a specific child, not an average child.

Match the words to the invoice. If the bill says "composite fee" and the page says "tuition," define the composite in one sentence. A mismatch here is how a careful school starts to feel slippery. The bursar and the website should share a noun.

## What sits outside the fee

The exclusions are part of the fit. Name them without apology and without a joke about "a few extras." Uniform, and whether it must be bought from one shop. Residential trips. Individual music lessons. Exam entries in the years they apply. A bus, if the bus is yours and billed. Damage, only if you actually charge it and the rule is explicable.

Put exclusions where the eye lands, not in a PDF linked as "further information." A parent comparing three schools will assume silence means included. When the second invoice arrives, the photograph of the classroom will not repair the feeling.

If an item is optional and common, give the shape, not a shrug. "Individual music lessons are arranged with visiting teachers and billed by them" is a shape. "Optional activities may incur charges" is a fog. Fog creates work for the office and doubt for the family.

Aid, bursary, or a sibling reduction belongs on this page if you offer it. Say who it is for, in plain language, and how a family starts that conversation. You do not need to publish a family's private award. You do need to stop implying that aid exists in a speech on open morning and nowhere on the site. If you do not offer aid, say that too. Silence reads as "maybe," and "maybe" generates inquiries you cannot answer well.

## The shape, not a puzzle

The shape is the pattern a family can learn in a minute. Annual fee by year group. What changes between years. What is billed per term if you bill per term, and how many terms. A deposit, and whether it is refundable, in one clause. The minute is the constraint implied by how little of a page gets read. Design for the minute.

Do not hide the annual number behind a termly figure that looks smaller, unless the termly figure is how you bill and the annual total sits in the same row. Parents multiply. Help them, or they will multiply wrong and feel you intended it. You probably did not. The page still did the harm.

A calculator that asks for an email before it shows a fee is a mailing list wearing a bursar costume. Skip it. The number is not a secret from the families you want. If the number is a secret, you do not have a pricing page. You have a reluctance, and the visit will go worse for it.

Years you no longer teach, or a pre-school you closed, should leave the table. Out-of-date fees are a worse mistake than a plain page, because they are a false promise with a pound sign. Date the page with the academic year. Update it when the board approves the new figure, not when the prospectus reprint happens to mention it.

If a fee changes for a new family and a returning family in the same year, say so. Two shapes, two lines. Blended language ("fees are set annually") without the two lines is how a current parent and a prospective parent compare notes and lose faith in both the site and the letter.

## From the fee to a visit or an inquiry

Every fee block needs the same next step. Visit, or inquire if a visit is not possible yet. The link should carry the age or year when you have more than one division, so a parent who has just understood the junior fee does not land in a senior open morning by accident.

Say what the visit will make concrete: the day they saw priced, not a different performance. If a conversation about aid should happen before a tour, say that beside the aid line, with the same reply window your office keeps. Do not promise a same-day award. Promise a real conversation with the person who can hold it.

A parent who is ready should not be sent back to the homepage to hunt for a date. The pricing page is often the second visit, or the page they forward to a partner. Treat it as a place where the decision can move. "Forward this to the person who handles the money" is a realistic use. The page should survive that forward without a spoken explanation from the parent who found it.

If you need a document for the accountant, link it after the human-readable table, and make the table sufficient on its own. A PDF that contradicts the HTML is two schools. Generate one from the other, or retire the PDF until it matches.

## What to stop writing

Stop the essay about education as an investment. The parent already believes education matters. They are trying to see the bill. A paragraph about the price of small classes does not replace the class size and the fee in one row. If small classes are why the fee is what it is, state the class size next to the fee. That is the argument, and it is checkable on a visit.

Stop the adjective stack. Outstanding, holistic, prestigious. None of those words changes the September number. If the school is small, the pricing page can say small, because small is part of fit and part of cost. Families who want small will stay. Families who need a huge range of labs will leave cleanly.

Stop a scholarship page that is only adjectives, linked from a fee table as if it were an answer. Either describe the kind of award, the rough shape, and how to inquire, or do not link it. A dead end under a fee is crueler than no link.

Read the page as if you were paying for a specific year. Circle every number. If a circle has no neighbor that says what it buys, write the neighbor. If a paragraph has no circle and no exclusion, ask whether it is doing a job. Most bursar prose is not.

## After the fee makes sense

A parent who understands the fee next wants each part of the day named with a boundary: the class, lunch, the end of the day, what you do not do. That is a services page, not a second tariff. [What each part of the school day includes, and where it stops](/blog/the-services-page-an-independent-school-actually-needs) is the next piece, because a price without those boundaries still leaves the comparison half done.

For a look at how clear offers get made visible, see [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Bring the fee sheet you already email. The page should be at least as honest as that sheet.
